question_text: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for joint pain following the acute onset of a diffuse, pruritic rash for the past 24 hours. A week ago, he was diagnosed with pharyngitis after returning home from summer camp and is currently taking antibiotics. There is no family history of serious illness. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows periorbital edema, generalized lymphadenopathy, and well-circumscribed, erythematous, confluent skin lesions of variable sizes up to several centimeters in width over his entire body. There is pain on passive movement of wrists and ankle joints bilaterally. Urine dipstick shows 1+ proteinuria. There is no hematuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Question
                    A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for joint pain following the acute onset of a diffuse, pruritic rash for the past 24 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

The most likely diagnosis is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) given the constellation of symptoms. The next step in management would involve supportive care and monitoring for APSGN rather than switching antibiotics or administering prednisone. Discontinuing the current antibiotic may be considered if it is suspected to be the cause of the reaction. Allergy testing or diphenhydramine administration is not indicated at this point.
